Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was the Indian lawyer who led the campaign for India's independence from British rule through mass nonviolent resistance. He lived from 1869 to 1948. "Mahatma" means "great soul", a title first given to him in 1914.

He grew up in a Hindu family in coastal Gujarat and trained as a lawyer in London. In 1893 he went to South Africa for a lawsuit and stayed 21 years. There, defending Indian migrants against racist laws, he worked out his method of satyagraha: open, disciplined refusal to obey unjust laws, accepting jail rather than striking back. Ideas from Tolstoy fed into it.

Back in India from 1915, he turned the Indian National Congress from a club of lawyers into a mass movement. His main campaigns against the British Raj:

  • Non-cooperation, 1920 to 1922: boycotts of British goods, courts and schools.
  • The Salt March of 1930: a 385 km walk to the sea to make salt, breaking the British salt tax.
  • Quit India, 1942: a call for the British to leave at once, which put him and the Congress leaders in jail for most of the war.

He spun his own cloth, wore a simple dhoti and campaigned against untouchability and for Hindu and Muslim unity. He failed to prevent the Partition of 1947 and spent its months fasting and walking through riot areas. A Hindu nationalist, Nathuram Godse, shot him dead in Delhi in January 1948. He had named Nehru his political heir. His methods later shaped Martin Luther King Jr. and Nelson Mandela.
